questions.q: Why does one Dockerfile in this lab produce two different images instead of needing two Dockerfiles?
options: A build arg (ENTRYPOINT_FILE) selects which file the final CMD runs, so the same build/runtime stages produce either image
Docker automatically detects how many services exist in src/
Kubernetes merges the two images back into one at deploy time
It doesn't -- a separate Dockerfile is required for each service
questions.explain: Passing --build-arg ENTRYPOINT_FILE at build time is what lets the same multi-stage Dockerfile produce the api image or the worker image.

questions.q: Why are the images tagged 1.0.0 instead of latest?
options: latest is required for Kubernetes to pull the image at all
1.0.0 makes the image build faster
If every push overwrites the same tag, there is no previous version left to roll back to -- a real version tag preserves that history
Tags have no effect on anything in this lab
questions.explain: Chapter 2 already covered this: latest being overwritten on every push is exactly why it makes rollback meaningless.

questions.q: Why doesn't the order-worker Deployment get its own Service?
options: Services are only allowed on Deployments with more than 2 replicas
Nothing in the cluster calls the worker over the network -- it only pulls from a queue, so a Service would be an unused object
Worker Deployments are never allowed to have Services in Kubernetes
A Service was created but deliberately left out of the YAML shown
questions.explain: Not every Deployment needs a Service; the worker only consumes from a queue and is never addressed directly, so it has none.

questions.q: What does the runtime stage of the Dockerfile base itself on, and why?
options: ubuntu:latest, for maximum compatibility
The same node:20-slim image used in the build stage, for consistency
A distroless Node.js image, running as the non-root user, so the shipped image has no shell or package manager
alpine, because it is required for all Node.js apps
questions.explain: The runtime stage copies only the built /app directory into a distroless base and drops to USER nonroot, per the Chapter 2 base-image lesson.

questions.q: Besides checking for errors, what is the real way to verify the api Deployment and Service are actually working?
options: Only checking that kubectl apply returned without an error message
Confirming every pod shows Running with READY 1/1, and that kubectl get endpoints order-api lists an endpoint for each pod
Restarting the cluster and seeing if it still boots
Checking the Dockerfile for typos one more time
questions.explain: Pods actually Running and Ready, plus the Service having real endpoints, is the real confirmation -- a clean apply alone doesn't prove anything is serving traffic.
